Our results address (i) the possible degrees of maps between arbitrary non-constant maps between fixed hyperbolicity over a fixed number field, (i the characteristic subfields of the source and target for such maps, (iii the fields of definition of the source and target, (iv the finiteness of the Jacobian varieties involved, (v the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the finiteness of the moduli spaces parameterizing these maps, (vi the fin

Transferring mannequin-to-robot capabilities is crucial for enabling robots to learn new tasks from humans. However, existing methods often struggle with difficult generalization when facing variations in anatomy or object characteristics. To address this, we introduce a new approach for transferring 3D manipulation capabilities by performing domain transformation. We begin by collecting manipulation capability datasets from both humans and robots through recording joint angles during demonstrations. Our method then aligns the human and robotic body configurations using manifold-aware Iterative Closest Point (ICM). During this alignment, we parallel transport the manipulation capability encoded in the human data onto the robot based on their respective joint angles. Finally, the robot learns a manipulation policy by imitating the derived human capability. Experiments conducted on XArm-5 and a NUCap human demonstrate that this manipulation capability transfer strategy outperforms previous methods.

This study applies the matrix element method to investigate signal extraction for the Higgs boson pair decay channel $\text{HH} \to \text{b}\bar{\text{b}}\text{W}\text{W}^{*}$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis focuses on the region where the Higgs mass lies between 115 and 160 GeV, utilizing both Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) and Leading Order (LO) simulation samples. The performance of various tagging strategies for b-jets and WW decays is evaluated. Furthermore, the study introduces a novel discriminant based on the matrix element method, demonstrating its superior effectiveness in enhancing the statistical significance of the observed signal.

Regenerative 3D vision methods typically depend on predefined 3D models or specific camera movement assumptions, whereas our approach utilizes a single uncalibrated image of an opaque object to predict its 3D pose and surface geometry. We introduce a technique that infers 3D models by simulating viewpoints through image-based rendering of rotations around an object's principal axes, utilizing a trainable turntable module to be precise. This method trains a decoder to regenerate images from these synthetic perspectives, allowing the resulting image discrepancies to estimate the objects 3D shapes and poses simultaneously. We have tested our method on the ShapeNet and FormNet datasets, demonstrating that it produces accurate results with a mean pose error of 12.5° and a root-mean-square shape error of 1.45 mm.

The rapid dissemination of misinformation on social media has fueled public fear and vaccine hesitancy, intensifying as the COVID-19 pandemic progressed. This study introduces a novel approach to identifying whether individuals accept or resist misinformation concerning the vaccine's safety and efficacy. We introduced an advanced framework that integrates both lexical and visual features to classify the acceptance status of misleading tweets about COVID-19 vaccines. Furthermore, we developed a new methodology capable of distinguishing acceptance from rejection of such misinformation in Twitter discourse. Leveraging this approach, we constructed the first-of-its-kind dataset, TwitterCoVax, comprising 20,000 tweets manually labeled by experts. Using this resource, we engineered two innovative models for detecting misinformational content in tweets: a BERT-based classifier and a visual feature detector. These models were applied to a specialized classifier trained to identify the acceptance status of integrated tweets. Our results demonstrate that the hybrid model, which combines textual and visual analysis, significantly outperforms text-only alternatives, achieving an F1-score of 0.8111 compared to 0.7641 for text-only approaches.

The interaction of intense terahertz fields with attosecond pulse trains (XUV) results in the isolation of a single, distinct XUV pulse. This occurs because the intense field induces a Doppler shift in the generated radiation, effectively breaking the periodic repetition typical of such interactions. This phenomenon enables the coherently controlled generation of isolated attosecond pulses, characterized by a tunable spectral content. Furthermore, such strong-field interactions allow for the manipulation of key attosecond pulse properties—including carrier-envelope phase, duration, and peak intensity—through the application of an external terahertz field.

The eclipsing binary Algol (Beta Persei) has long served as a fundamental model for low-mass main-sequence stars interacting with higher-mass companions in eclipsing configurations. Recent high-precision photometric and spectroscopic data have uncovered periodic variations in Algol's characteristics, prompting hypotheses regarding either a third celestial body or magnetic activity as the cause. This study introduces fresh high-precision $V$-band photometry and $H\alpha$ spectroscopic data for the system, analyzed using both the "jitter" method and the Coherence Function. These findings reveal a clear 3.9-day periodicity, offering compelling evidence for the presence of a secondary magnetic field or a tertiary star. To evaluate this, we conducted a comprehensive search for potential third-star candidates, utilizing Gaia EDR3 parallaxes and proper motions alongside ground-based high-resolution spectroscopy for radial velocity measurements. By combining these datasets, we identified a specific region in the system's parameter space containing 11 viable candidates that satisfy all necessary physical constraints.

We investigate the nonlinear Dirac equation in the exterior of a smooth, bounded, and strictly convex obstacle situated in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, imposing nonlinear growth conditions on the power exponent $p$ within the interval $1 < p < 25$. By employing the linking method alongside a linking constant $C_{link}$, we demonstrate the existence of a solution pair $(u, v)$ such that $\|u\|_{L^p} > \delta$ for some $\delta > 0$, thereby confirming the existence of "explosion" solutions that concentrate at the obstacle's boundary as the nonlinear parameter approaches its critical threshold.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have proven effective for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) across various fields, though their computational cost can be prohibitive for high-dimensional problems or those with complex PDEs and boundary conditions. While node-free PINN implementations often require a dense mesh of data points to ensure convergence, this paper introduces a novel adaptive strategy for efficient PINN training. By leveraging a mesh of nodes to guide the process, we propose a new adaptive method that refines training data points based on a residual-driven criterion. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that this approach significantly reduces training time compared to the standard static training procedure.

This research investigates multi-domain formation within ferroelectric body and gate-stack structures of nanoscale field-effect transistors. Utilizing a first-principles-based phenomenological approach, we analyze the impact of these internal domains on switching characteristics and hysteresis loops. Our findings reveal that walls located in the substrate generate an adverse capacitance, exerting a pronounced influence on multi-domain evolution and switching dynamics. We further examine how variations in electrode work functions, thickness, and ferroelectric composition contribute to intrinsic profile adjustments and multi-domain reconfiguration.

The cargo ecosystem has grown increasingly intricate, making it difficult for stakeholders to fully comprehend inter-cargo relationships and their impact on the network's overall structure. This study introduces a Dependency-Weakness Knowledge Graph (DKG) designed to map both the interconnectedness and inherent frailties within the network. The research further examines the propagation of vulnerabilities through cargo dependencies utilizing a Monte Carlo method, while also introducing the Propagation Strength metric to assess potential risk levels. The application of the DKG and subsequent vulnerability propagation analysis were conducted on real-world port cargo data from the Port of Shanghai. The findings reveal that nearly 70% of all cargo items possess at least one dependency, with approximately 30% acting as critical links supporting multiple other goods. The propagation analysis indicates that although most cargo face less than a 10% risk of being compromised, certain high-stakes items face risks exceeding 50%. Ultimately, the DKG framework and the propagation assessment method provide a robust means of identifying latent weaknesses and anticipating potential disruptions within the cargo ecosystem.

This study examines the irreducibility of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equations subject to pure jump noise. By employing the strong Feller property and establishing the existence of a positive solution to an associated backward Kolmogorov equation, we demonstrate the irreducibility of the corresponding Markov semigroup. These findings are utilized to prove the existence of an invariant measure for the corresponding stochastic dynamics. Furthermore, by leveraging the ergodicity of the resulting Markov processes, we determine the precise growth rate of solutions.

For a group $G$, its minimum order power graph, denoted $\MinOut(G)$, refers to a minimal subgraph (regarding the number of edges) of the power graph that remains isomorphic to a power graph of some group $G'$. The quantity $\MinOut(G)$ is defined as the edge count of this minimal graph. In this paper, we derive the order of $\MinOut(G)$ for certain power groups of finite nilpotent groups and derive conditions for when this value equals the order of the original group $G$. Additionally, the authors present a characterization of power groups of finite $p$-groups that are minimal power groups of some group $G'$ (i.e., $G'$ power group is isomorphic to $G'$).

This paper introduces the HADEX concept, a proposed hadron spectrometer designed for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). HADEX aims to conduct comprehensive studies of hadron production and transport across all phases of phase space, achieving this through precise measurements of both the momentum and rapidity of individual hadrons and (anti-)nuclei. The device employs time-of-flight techniques within an extensive detector volume to deliver superior acceptance for light particles while maintaining excellent momentum resolution for heavy masses. Additionally, it offers robust coverage for high transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) regions using time-of-flight data complemented by silicon detectors and scintillating fiber tracking. The instrument's capabilities for measuring hadronic transverse momentum distributions are examined, along with its potential to determine spectra for various species, particularly at high $p_{\mathrm{T}}$. Furthermore, its utility in analyzing non-equilibrium effects during the hadronization process and hadron recombination models is explored. The paper concludes by outlining the in-situ calibration strategies required for the device and assessing its potential contributions to measurements of heavy-ion collisions.

This paper introduces Directional Convolutional Networks (DCNets), a new framework for image recognition that employs directional convolutions to analyze images across multiple orientations. While the initial version, IS-DCN, applies this operation at the input layer, the authors also developed a more efficient variant, AP-DCN, which integrates the operation directly into the convolutional layers. AP-DCN matches the performance of the initial version while requiring significantly fewer parameters and maintaining a compact architecture. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that both models outperform standard convolutional networks using fewer filters, thereby reducing computational costs for image recognition.

Point cloud data, which captures the three-dimensional geometry of real-world objects, is extensively utilized in computer vision and robotics applications. However, existing Point Cloud Convolutional Networks (PCNs) often struggle with limited expressiveness and training efficiency. This study introduces an enhanced Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) architecture designed to effectively process point cloud information while enhancing both model expressiveness and learning efficiency. The proposed method constructs dynamic neighborhood relationships around each point by establishing a k-d tree, utilizing graph-based convolutions to extract local geometric features, and applying global feature fusion techniques to handle point dependencies across the entire cloud. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets confirm that this architecture outperforms current state-of-the-art point cloud processing models in classification and semantic segmentation tasks.

The primary objective of this study is to introduce a semantics-based, host-independent Trojan architecture for deep learning models. Existing remote Trojan methods rely on specific host environments to tailor adversarial triggers, limiting their portability; conversely, our host-independent Semantic Host-less Trojans (SHTs), implemented via SHTNet, automatically generate triggers without such reliance, ensuring direct transferability to targeted devices. These semantics-driven, host-less Trojans encode trigger patterns within the injected network backbones using a back-translation technique. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art remote architectures in accuracy, attack success rates, and resource efficiency, achieving a 99.2% success rate for a 10-layer ResNet with merely a 0.05% accuracy drop.

In 2018, the Magellan Baade telescope began operations with the refurbished Multi-object Spectrograph And Image System (MAGIS). This upgrade included a new Reduction System for Observational Image Extraction (ROSIE) pipeline and a new Integral Field Device (ROSIE-IFU), enabling observations using both traditional spectroscopy and IFU capabilities. Located at the Maglad Control Room, the ROSIE pipeline manages all observer-submitted programs covering IFU and spectroscopic observations from the Maglad instrument. Designed to support diverse observational modes, the system handles data reduction for long-slit, multi-obj, IFU, and image modes. This paper outlines the instrument's design and explains the specific adaptations made to ROSIE to facilitate IFU observations.

This study examines the fusion of two $^{12}$C nuclei at extremely low energies, specifically focusing on the entrance channel involving the $^{12}$C-$^{12}$C cluster system. We analyze the current state of fusion research at these subbarrier levels and explore future prospects, including how the Trojan Horse Method (THM) can advance the field. Additionally, we present recent findings from a newly developed variant of the THM designed for low-energy fusion investigations. This approach utilizes a deuterium-$^{12}$C two-body system as the entrance configuration, effectively treating deuterium as a "spectator." By measuring the final state where a proton is ejected alongside the formation of a compound nucleus in the exit channel, this setup enables the indirect reconstruction of the fusion process through the study of three-body interactions.

We present high-resolution, high-signal-to-noise-ratio spectra for eight planet-hosting stars (G2V-G8V) spanning effective temperatures of 5200–5600 K, covering the wavelength range from 4700 to 6800 Å. Our analysis employs spectral synthesis to derive precise abundances for 14 elements (C, N, O, Na, Mg, Si, S, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, and Ni) and to determine the stellar microturbulence ($v_{\text{t}}$) and microdifferential parameters ($\varepsilon_{\text{gr}}$, $\varepsilon_{\text{gr}}$, $\varepsilon_{\text{gr}}$). These data allow us to calculate precise stellar chemical compositions and assess their homogeneity. We also examine the correlation between stellar metallicity and the masses of orbiting planets. Furthermore, we model the internal compositions of terrestrial exoplanets, estimating their core mass fractions and core radii under the assumption that planetary material mirrors stellar abundances. Our findings indicate that exoplanets with masses between 0.5 and 2.5 $M_{\oplus}$ likely possess differentiated structures with iron cores, though the specific core mass fraction varies by system.

Deep learning techniques utilizing channel state information (CSI) have proven highly effective for wireless localization. Nevertheless, standard deep learning models often demand extensive labeled datasets to cover diverse environmental changes and user movements, which are costly and time-consuming to acquire. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a localization framework based on enhanced CSI deep neural networks (DDC-CSI DDPL), which integrates a multi-head attention mechanism to boost localization accuracy. Specifically, the system employs a multi-head attention layer within the fully connected segments of the classifier to better capture critical radio frequency characteristics. This approach ensures efficient learning from limited labeled data by improving feature representation. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed architecture achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving resource-constrained training datasets.

We introduce a common framework for various modal logics using the categorical properties of Stone and Hausdorff spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that property-based Stone duality serves as the logical foundation for modal reasoning by providing an alternative to traditional Kripke semantics. In this context, the modal operators correspond to specific continuous maps between the associated Stone spaces, while modal axioms reflect the topological characteristics of these spaces. We establish the soundness and completeness of this topological Semantics with respect to the modal syntax, with the results remaining valid across different varieties of modal systems.

A graph's edge-chromatic number, denoted as $\chi'(G)$, represents the minimal count of colors required for a proper edge coloring of $G$. For any graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, Vizing's Theorem establishes that $\Delta(G) \leq \chi'(G) \leq \Delta(G)+1$. Consequently, edge colorings of graphs with degree two are well-established, whereas the classification of high-degree graphs remains an open challenge. This study focuses on robust edge colorings, defined as colorings where recoloring a minimal set of edges allows a transformation from any given edge coloring to a complete one. While previous research has largely addressed robust colorings in degree-two networks, this work presents a significant advancement by constructing a counterexample in cubic bipartite graphs. Specifically, we identify a 12-vertex bipartite graph that cannot achieve full edge-coloring robustness.

Griggs and Ruzsa (1992) demonstrated that any function $f$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ with a Fourier coefficient $\hat f(k)$ exceeding $1/2$ at some index $k$ must possess a mean value $\hat f(0)$ no greater than $1/2 - \delta$ for some $\delta > 0$. This finding was later broadened to Hamming graphs $H(d,n)$ by Linial, Radcliffe, Spener, and Spencer (1995). In this paper, we further generalize these results to functions defined on arbitrary finite Abelian groups. Specifically, we determine the infimum possible value for $\hat f(0)$ given a constraint that $\hat f(k) \geq \alpha$ for some element $k$ in the group, where $\alpha$ is a specified constant.

COPASI, a widely used cross-platform simulation tool for biochemical pathways, has seen significant growth in its web-based services, which now include HTTP API access for model submission, retrieval, and the execution of basic simulations. In contrast, ShinyCOPASI introduces a distinct approach by offering a web-based user interface tailored for interactive investigation of COPASI models. Leaning on the Shiny framework for dynamic web apps, it seamlessly integrates file uploads, control panels, and results visualization. This interface supports multiple output formats, allowing users to view data either graphically or in tabular form directly in a web browser.

Scientific Machine Learning (SML) leverages neural networks to solve inverse and direct problems in science by learning mappings from data, a process that inherently introduces uncertainties due to factors like limited data, model architecture, and hyperparameters. This study presents an extensive comparison of uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for SML, evaluating twelve different approaches for both predictive tasks and inverse problems using standard benchmark datasets. The authors analyze the impacts of data volume, architecture, and hyperparameters on SML uncertainty estimates, revealing that while deep uncertainty estimates in SML mirror those in standard supervised learning, the expected sharpness of SML conditional probability distributions often degrades. Additionally, the proposed Entropy-based Uncertainty (EUI) method demonstrates particular promise for addressing inverse problems.

The authors investigate the von Neumann algebras generated by category functions on a compact quantum group. In cases where these algebras turn out to be abelian, the underlying quantum groups are identified.

Imprecise probability models are increasingly favored for representing uncertainty in information regarding a system's transition dynamics within Markov chains. To address this, researchers have developed GMRES-like iterative algorithms capable of approximating the stationary distribution for such models. However, integrating this computational approach with Markov Decision Process (MDP) policy iteration remains an open challenge. This paper introduces a novel imprecise GMRES policy iteration method designed to scale effectively to large MDPs. By leveraging GMRES for large Markov models in conjunction with a highly efficient acceleration technique known as the Chebyshev trick, we demonstrate through both synthetic and real-world case studies that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing alternatives in terms of computational speed.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. This study investigates both the strongly connected components and the underlying structure of $\mathcal{D}$ to determine a sufficient condition ensuring that the typical and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ coincide.

This study addresses the inverse problem of estimating unknown parameters within time-series computer models when direct access to output values is unavailable due to high simulation costs. To overcome these expenses, a novel Bayesian framework utilizing a composite likelihood autocorrelation function as a surrogate is proposed. The method employs Multiple Contour Estimation (MCE)—an alternative to Markov Chain Monte Carlo—for jointly inferring the latent state sequence and the model's autocorrelation parameters. The efficiency of this approach is validated through multiple numerical experiments, including an application to reconstructing the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) dynamics using the time-series output from the NCAR CCSM4 climate simulator.

Local inquiries are a cornerstone technique in robust learning, yet existing literature offers limited guidance on their utility for achieving robust generalization. This work addresses that gap by establishing theoretical guarantees for local inquiries within the context of generalization bounds for robust errors. Our findings indicate that local inquiries prove beneficial in generalization only when they are paired with an appropriate representation learning strategy. Specifically, we demonstrate that combining local inquiries with dropout offers theoretical advantages in robust generalization for convex problems. Additionally, we provide extensive experimental results on robust classification tasks for image and text data, which support our theoretical findings.

This study reports the initial measurement of medium-induced modifications to jet fragmentation within Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, utilizing CMS detector data from the LHC. The analysis focuses on reconstructing jets in high-transverse-momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) photon-tagged events across various rapidity bins, covering both central and forward regions. The observed alterations in jet substructure are consistent with expectations for a strongly interacting quark-gluon plasma, aligning with previous findings that tag jets without a specific isolated photon.

Building on the methodology from reference [10], we derive several Apéry-type series featuring alternating signs and mixed index parities on the summation side. These results express terms involving products of alternating harmonic numbers alongside colored multiple zeta functions (C-MZF). Consequently, our findings yield numerous new identities concerning Apéry-type alternating series and establish fresh values for alternating special series, including harmonic number products.

This study presents the findings of a follow-up spectroscopic and photometric investigation into the enigmatic brown dwarf WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, commonly referred to as "The Mishap." Initially, this object was classified as a peculiar T4 spectral binary system with an unusually wide separation of 1.2 arcseconds; however, initial analysis suggested a misclassification. Our observations reveal that the system is actually a single object exhibiting a unique spectrum characterized by a distinct lack of methane absorption and unusual molecular features. We have determined that the system is a visual binary with a projected angular separation of 0.04 arcseconds and a lower limit for its orbital period exceeding 1.5 years. By comparing the object's spectral characteristics to the M and T dwarf spectral sequence, we infer a classification of M9.5, a mass of 0.025 M$_{\odot}$, and an age greater than 1.5 years. Furthermore, we have measured the radial velocities of both components, finding values of -10.6 $\pm$ 0.2 km s$^{-1}$ for the primary and -10.1 $\pm$ 0.2 km s$^{-1}$ for the secondary, with no significant difference between them. The companion displays a spectrum resembling a T6 dwarf, yet its radial velocity tracks the primary's, indicating that the original binary nature

This study presents the production yields of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons in central Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV, utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. The results are analyzed in terms of transverse mass ($m_{\rm T}$) and rapidity ($y$), alongside ratios of these quantities for various particle species. These findings are compared against predictions from various theoretical models. The analysis reveals that the measured Xe-Xe particle ratios align well with predictions from the extended Hadron Resonance Gas (HRG) model, which incorporates contributions from hadronic resonances.

We introduce a method for parton distribution function (PDF) evolution and interpolation that leverages effective field theory within a basis of J/ Schemer effective operators. The resulting parametric PDF forms are expressed as linear combinations of these effective functions, with coefficients determined by fitting to experimental data. The study demonstrates the application of this approach in interpolating and evolving both unpolarized and polarized PDFs across a wide range of momentum scales ($Q^2$) from 0.01 to $10^4$ GeV$^2$.

This study investigates how sintering temperature affects the microstructure and mechanical properties of pressed agglomerates made from Martian and lunar regolith. We examined regolith samples collected by Apollo 17 on the Moon and the Perseverance rover at Jezero Crater on Mars. Results indicate that increasing sintering temperatures enhance both density and compressive strength. Additionally, we analyzed the mechanical behavior of these airagglomerates by measuring their Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and fracture toughness. Microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was conducted to explore the correlation between microstructure and mechanical performance. The findings suggest that optimal regolith agglomerates for 3D printing should be sintered at temperatures between 600°C and 800°C.

This study examines the onset of Rayleigh-Plateau instability within a liquid film coating a cylindrical fiber, with a specific focus on how slip at the liquid-fiber interface influences the emergence of primary droplets. The governing equations, adapted from Pearson's classic work on falling films, were modified to incorporate boundary conditions reflecting interfacial slip. Results indicate that increasing slip intensity amplifies growth rates across all instability wavelengths, with the most significant impact observed on shorter wavenumbers. Furthermore, higher slip enhances the initial amplification stage, causing the instability to favor even shorter wavelengths more strongly. By analyzing the transition from linear growth to non-linear saturation, we demonstrated that slip accelerates saturation, yielding smaller droplets. Finally, the predicted slip-driven variations in onset frequency and drop size were compared against existing experimental data.

The star formation rate (SFR) is a fundamental metric for characterizing a galaxy's evolution. While the dust-attenuated emission from young stars is traditionally used to derive SFRs, this method introduces uncertainties that are difficult to quantify. Consequently, we utilized the Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$) line—a tracer of mid-infrared recombination radiation—to assess the reliability of SFR estimates. Our study focused on 100 star-forming galaxies with redshifts $z < 0.05$ and available data from the GAMA survey, which included both photometry and spectroscopy. We measured Br$\gamma$ line luminosities and compared them against SFR predictions generated from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. The results indicate a strong correlation between the two, with a scatter of only 0.3 dex. This Br$\gamma$ luminosity serves as an independent SFR indicator, largely immune to dust extinction, and offers a straightforward spectroscopic validation for SED-derived results.

This article is the first in a two-part study focused on classifying tensor idempotants within the category of regionally based $\mathscr{sl}_M$ (for $M > N > 2$, and of type $II$) quantum affine groups $R^i_j$. The authors establish a correspondence linking symmetries of these tensor idempotants to a specific subgroup of $S_{M-N+2} \times S_N$. The required properties of the idempotants, which are constructed from transfer matrices, will be addressed in the subsequent paper.

This paper introduces a new direct approach for solving direct absorption equations, showing that the method successfully generates new solutions from existing ones while strictly preserving positivity. Its versatility is demonstrated through applications to both Green's functions and time-elapsed diffusion processes, ultimately proving effective for these broad categories of diffraction problems.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is a well-established technology widely used globally to convert images of printed text into machine-processable digital data. In contrast, detecting handwritten content, particularly complex mathematical formulas, remains a difficult and largely unresolved challenge. This study introduces a novel system designed to accurately identify and classify written mathematical expressions. The proposed methodology employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract salient features from raw pen-stroke data, followed by a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to perform expression detection based on these extracted characteristics. The model was rigorously evaluated using data collected from participants who completed the Expressions Detection Task on a tablet, utilizing an integrated stylus pressure and position sensor. The resulting dataset comprises 100 distinct mathematical expressions annotated with corresponding stroke information. The achieved performance yielded an accuracy of 92.8%, an F1 score of 92.6%, an precision of 92.6%, and an recall of 92.6%.

Speech duration is a fundamental element in the transcription phase, which is essential for effective speech recognition. In this paper, we address the generation of synthetic speech lengths from original audio recordings. We employ a non-parametric, data-driven methodology to enhance the synthesis of speech durations. We demonstrate the generation of synthetic speech durations using a simple yet effective statistical technique. We also discuss the importance of these synthesized speech durations in the context of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). We show that these synthesized speech durations can be used to augment existing training sets for neural network models. We illustrate that augmenting training sets with synthesized speech durations improves the ASR system's robustness to variations in speech duration. Spatial presence models (SPMs) are increasingly utilized in ecological research to analyze species distribution data while accounting for spatial dependencies. The `spOccupancy` R package is designed to fit SPMs for single-species data, as well as for multi-species data using independent, joint, or integrated frameworks. We provide an overview of the package's functionalities, its spatial covariates, and the various SPM specifications supported. We demonstrate the software using realistic examples, visualize model diagnostics, and evaluate performance through a simulation study. Additionally, `spOccupancy` includes functions for spatial cross-validation and post-holding analysis, such as identifying spatial clusters. The package is available on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=spOccupancy.

The Skincare initiative, introduced in 2019, is dedicated to the research, development, and deployment of a clinical decision support system for diagnosing cutaneous lesions. The project's vision is to create an accessible, user-friendly, and cost-effective tool that improves the differential diagnosis of skin conditions, particularly for dermatologists and nurses. The system relies on a technical architecture combining a computer vision-driven, deep learning-based diagnostic engine with a user interface tailored for clinicians. This user-centric design prioritizes practicality, ensuring seamless daily integration into medical practice. The interface emphasizes transparency and explainability, ensuring clinicians can understand and trust the system's recommendations. Furthermore, the core diagnostic algorithms are built upon the industry-standard ISIC 2019 dataset, which contains 11,000 images of skin lesions.

We introduce a probabilistic autoencoder designed to forecast future spectra for Type Ia supernovae, utilizing data exclusively from the Zwicky Transient Survey. These deep generative models are capable of learning latent representations of complex nonlinear relationships within Type Ia supernovae spectral data. By training the network to predict future spectral states, we can assess the model's reliability through validation against actual observations. Our results indicate that a future spectrum generated by our Probabilistic AutoEncoder (PAE) achieves a correlation coefficient of 0.95 compared to real observations, demonstrating a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we explore potential applications of the PAE in forecasting future events for other transient astronomical phenomena.

We present deep, multi-wavelength data (from 0.3 to 24 μm) for a dusty starbursting galaxy located at z = 2.09, which exhibits a gravitational lensing magnification factor of μ = 10.5 ± 0.5. Our analysis reveals a resolved, bipolar neutral outflow with a diameter of approximately 1.5 kpc and a mass of roughly 10⁹ M☉. The outflowing gas moves at velocities between 150 and 200 km s⁻¹, with a surface mass density of about 0.001 M☉ pc⁻². This outflow is driven by intense starburst activity, evidenced by a star formation rate (SFR) of 1000 M☉ yr⁻¹ and a total stellar mass of 1.5 × 10¹⁰ M☉. The observed neutral gas mass is roughly 100 times the current star formation rate, indicating that the bulk of the ejected material has not yet been expelled from the galaxy. Comparatively, the outflow's mass and momentum generation rates are exceptionally high, exceeding typical values by factors of 100 and 1,000 respectively. While the outflow's specific momentum generation is too low to efficiently clear the galaxy, its immense power suggests it can effectively disperse the interstellar medium and drive substantial chemical

This study introduces a new analytical model describing the entrainment of an ambient fluid into particle-laden turbulent plumes, which are generated by localized sources within stratified environments. The proposed entrainment velocity results from balancing turbulent kinetic energy dissipation with enstrophy production, a mechanism that aligns closely with recent theoretical frameworks for clean (particle-free) plumes. Additionally, the model defines the entrainment-driven growth rate of the plume radius by equating the time derivative of plume momentum to the entrainment force. These theoretical predictions were validated against direct numerical simulations featuring finite-sized heavy particle sources in homogeneous fluids, demonstrating strong agreement across the entire evolution. The results reveal that increasing the Stokes number leads to enhanced both the density-driven entrainment velocity and the subsequent radius expansion.

The spread of infectious diseases within a population is frequently modeled as a Markov process that, in the limit of large populations, converges to a branching process characterized by the same limiting one-step transition probabilities. For a general measure of infection risk, we determine the critical value of the spectral radius of a specific matrix that dictates whether the disease faces extinction or persists. In the case of homogeneous risk, this critical threshold corresponds to the spectral radius of the hypergraph's adjacency operator, which is modified by the risk's third moment. Furthermore, when risk depends on the size of the largest neighborhood within the underlying hypergraph, the threshold relates to the spectral radius of the pertiau-enrolled (or perturbed) hypergraph Laplacian.

The atomic-scale spin configuration of the CrI3 monolayer is characterized by an out-of-plane orientation, yet its bilayer form, which exhibits a ferromagnetic state with non-centrosymmetry, has recently been reported to display complex in-plane textures. This study utilizes ab initio calculations to investigate the origins of such intricate spin arrangements within the bilayer structure. We attribute these complex textures to a combination of the intrinsic out-of-plane spin component and Rashba-like terms arising from the lack of central symmetry. Furthermore, we examine the roles of magnetic anisotropy and spin-orbit coupling in determining the spin architecture, while also exploring how structural distortions and external fields can manipulate these complex textures.

Differential rotation serves as a primary driver of magnetic activity in solar-type stars, specifically through its influence on the small-scale dynamo and the generation of large-scale magnetic fields via mean-field dynamos. In the Sun, the differential rotation profile exhibits a characteristic "anti-solar" behavior at low latitudes during the solar minimum, featuring a local extremum in the angular velocity distribution. This phenomenon is hypothesized to be a direct outcome of large-scale magnetic cycles. Consequently, this "anti-solar" profile is absent in rapidly rotating stars, which generally display a monotonic decrease in angular velocity from the equator toward the poles. Focusing on stars with rotation periods exceeding 20 days, this study investigates the impact of such anti-solar differential rotation within mean-field dynamo models. We demonstrate that incorporating this "anti-solar" profile can successfully explain the observed large-scale magnetic cycles in solar analogs, particularly the generation of magnetic polar reversals and the generation of extended magnetic grand minima.

We introduce a novel K-fan multimodal deep framework designed to integrate information from K distinct data sources. Key to our approach is a generalized K-fan structure that enables the combination of various kernel functions, allowing simultaneous processing of dissimilar modalities such as graphs, images, and text. To ensure effective feature sharing, we employ a symmetric weight strategy within the architecture. Furthermore, we utilize a multi-task learning approach to jointly represent all modalities in a common space, optimizing the framework with the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss function. Our evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing multimodal models.

Dynamic partial order reduction (DPOR) serves as a dominant approach for detecting concurrency bugs in multi-threaded programs. Although earlier DPOR models were restricted to basic constructs like locks and condition variables, recent advancements have expanded their applicability to higher-level primitives such as semaphores, mutexes, and atomic operations. This study introduces a new DPOR model designed for programs utilizing both basic and advanced synchronization mechanisms, leveraging the McMini abstract machine for mcrl2. This combination enables the McMini tool to generate more compact partial order traces, substantially lowering the volume of program states required for correctness verification. Furthermore, McMini offers a declarative framework that allows researchers to easily integrate support for additional synchronization primitives.

The rapid dissemination of false information via social media and messaging platforms has prompted these platforms to implement measures to curb message forwarding. WhatsApp recently announced a policy change to restrict forwarding to only five messages at once, a limitation users can only bypass three times per hour. This study investigates the impact of such policies on the distribution of inaccurate information. Our findings indicate that while these interventions may slightly reduce the total volume of shared misinformation, they fail to substantially alter prevailing narratives or significantly decrease the overall scale of information contagion.

The study examines a model of branching population dynamics featuring a diverse supercritical reproduction mechanism and a diverse set of initial alleles. The branching process is defined by a diverse probability-generating function (pgf), $f(s)$, where $f''(1)$ represents the variance in offspring number and $f'(1)-1$ signifies the expected surplus offspring. The initial allele distribution is described by the frequency $p$. The research analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the branching population's allelic frequency distribution as time $t$ approaches infinity. The approximations for this distribution are derived from the diverse probability-generating function, $f(s)$, specifically its second derivative at unity, $f''(1)$, and its expansion around $s=1$. The expected number of alleles with frequency exceeding $x$ is approximated using a diverse function, $g(x)$, defined as:

where $g(s)$ represents the diverse probability-generating function, $f(s)$, evaluated at $s=1-x$. The diverse probability-generating function, $f(s)$, is assumed to be diverse and increasing on $[0,1]$, with $f''(1)$ representing the variance in offspring number and $f'(1)-1$ representing the expected surplus offspring. Deep learning techniques have proven highly effective in distinguishing between authentic and spoofed speech, yet they often struggle with generalization across different tasks and demonstrate limited performance when facing unseen speaker voices or novel recording conditions. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a specialized neural network component called the Attentive Activation Mechanism (AAM), designed to enhance the innate generalization capabilities of end-to-end spoofing detection models. Evaluations across three distinct databases confirm that AAM significantly boosts generalization performance; specifically, on the ANTI-VOICEPRINT CHALLENGE 2020 dataset, it yielded a relative improvement of 10.4% in Equal Error Rate (EER).

We examine global supersymmetric effective field models for inflation, wherein supersymmetry is preserved within inflaton fluctuations but broken at the scale defining the vacuum. In this framework, inflaton dynamics are governed by an expansion of the kinetic and potential terms by powers of the field relative to the supersymmetry-breaking scale. We identify that, unlike in non-global setups, global $U(1)$ symmetries can stabilize the inflaton mass at leading order. Additionally, we compare canonical normalizations of the kinetic terms and analyze how unquantified higher-dimensional operators influence inflaton fluctuations and reheating mechanisms following inflation.

Photon pair correlation measurements are essential for validating quantum optics theories and validating entanglement. This study reports on the unexpected asymmetry found in the second-order correlation functions of entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. The observed asymmetry results from the intrinsic type-II non-linear non-linear crystal geometry, interacting with the array of detection apertures and the specific polarization states of the generated pairs. Although the effect is most prominent when using a multi-aperture system, it also influences the correlation profile recorded in a standard two-aperture setup.

Superconducting quantum circuits are a primary focus of current quantum information research. However, unavoidable material defects cause decoherence, limiting quantum processing to roughly 100 operations. To address this, strategies to identify and eliminate flaws are essential. This study utilizes terahertz scanning microscopy to examine native defects within superconductors used for fabricating microwave resonators on lithographically defined planar spiral inductors. By measuring the spectral resonance shifts of these circuits, we correlate specific defect locations with microscopic impurities and analyze their interaction mechanisms. Furthermore, we explore how our imaging results influence resonance properties when coupled with adjustable spiral inductors, ultimately demonstrating near-field terahertz nanoscopy as a powerful tool for mapping intrinsic defects in thin-film superconductors.

When two Borel sets on the real line intersect to form a countable collection, at least one of these sets must contain a non-empty open interval. Consequently, any partitioning of the real axis into Borel sets can consist of no more than a countable number of elements; however, this specific result and the broader question of whether every such partition necessarily is countable have historically lacked a direct constructive proof. This discussion provides an explicit example—specifically, a partition composed of disjoint closed sets with vacuous interiors that demonstrates and validates the stated intersection property, thereby reinforcing the underlying mathematical conclusion.

The paper examines the performance of introducing new investment strategies alongside currently active trading tactics. We employ an agent-based model featuring diverse trading agents, each governed by specific market entry and exit rules. By simulating the stock market with a single new trading agent added to an established population, we investigate the impact of adding new investment approaches on the returns of existing agents. Our findings indicate that the collective outcome depends heavily on the specific nature of the introduced strategy. We analyze the results across two scenarios: continuous investment and periodic investment, further breaking them down into continuous reinvestment versus continuous or conditional investment in new positions. The study assesses how these introduction methods affect the profits of existing agents, their investment frequency, and the overall market's volatility.

Dynamic protocol detection involves a network security monitoring tool (NSM) analyzing a device's established connection parameters, such as the applications running on it, by observing the cryptographic handshakes of the protocol used for the communication. This capability allows the NSM to maintain a record of detected applications, thereby alerting the user to any that are unknown. While dynamic detection offers significant benefits, this paper examines current assaults targeting this feature specifically in relation to the open-source tools Zeek and Snort. The study begins by outlining the fundamental principles of dynamic protocol detection and then analyzes how specific vulnerabilities in both Zeek and Snort can be exploited. The authors present various attack strategies, including the falsification of handshakes to mimic legitimate application traffic and the insertion of malicious code into NSM configuration files.

The interaction between magnons and the effective action of proximitizing superconductors are examined. By employing the Fermi-Dirac distribution, a temperature-dependent effective gate is demonstrated, allowing for the thermal control of magnon density. Additionally, the analysis reveals that magnetization modulation via the superconducting state, rather than temperature, is possible when magnons couple with phonons.

Federated Learning (FL) offers a secure approach to distributed machine learning by distributing data across local nodes, yet it faces significant challenges when new classes emerge at participating clients, particularly in a zero-shot setting where no training data for those novel categories is available. To address this issue, the authors introduce a novel zero-shot FL framework designed for audio classification. The system integrates a local classification module at each client to identify and localize newly appeared audio categories without prior training data, alongside a global strategy to harmonize these discoveries across all participants. Crucially, FL model parameters remain unupdated during this zero-shot adaptation phase, thereby preventing performance degradation on existing tasks. The effectiveness of this method is validated through experiments on the YTF-10 dataset, demonstrating superior results compared to baseline FL approaches.

The primary goal of this study is the full quantum state tomography (QST) of the $|0\rangle^{\otimes n}$-GHZ states across $n$ qubits (where $n \in \{2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$). These highly entangled GHZ states are constructed using superposition techniques applied to $n$-qubit product states. We evaluate the fidelity between the experimentally reconstructed quantum states and the theoretical models derived from the QST procedures.

Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) are emerging as a promising auxiliary technology to enhance network coverage and spectral efficiency through user-specific beamforming. By optimally adjusting the metasurface's reflective coefficients, IRS can significantly boost communication link reliability. This study investigates a practical implementation where an IRS assists a multi-user scenario involving a Multiple-Input Single-Output system, focusing specifically on low-complexity channel estimation. To address this, the authors propose a cascaded estimation method divided into two phases: first, jointly determining the active user indices and IRS phase shifts via a message passing algorithm; second, estimating the channels for the identified active users using Pilot Assisted Minimum Mean Square Error (PAMMSE). Simulation results demonstrate that the suggested message passing-based approach achieves performance nearly equivalent to full-complexity pilot-assisted minimum mean square error (PMMSE) methods while drastically reducing computational complexity.

This research investigates how local U.S. news online coverage of the pandemic responded to case and death counts, while simultaneously examining the correlation between news volume and public concern. Data were sourced from 244 American news outlets, identified through an audience survey, with news coverage quantified by scraping over 1.5 million articles from more than 140 websites. The study employed a Poisson regression model to analyze the drivers of news coverage and a mixed-effects logistic regression to assess whether exposure to this information correlated with heightened public anxiety. Findings indicate that local news outlets significantly increased their reporting on the COVID-19 crisis as U.S. infections and fatalities escalated. Furthermore, greater exposure to COVID-19 news was associated with increased public worry, even after adjusting for individual demographics and regional characteristics.

We introduce a novel framework that utilizes a memory-augmented neural network to investigate how humans acquire the ability to count. This approach is grounded in prior research indicating that the acquisition of counting relies on abstract principles capable of being applied to both artificial intelligence systems and the human mind. The proposed system successfully simulates human counting development, accurately capturing key phenomena such as the capacity to count objects of varying quantities, the capability to continue a counting sequence, and the acquisition of stable, consistent counts. Furthermore, the framework enables the systematic examination of individual differences in learning, specifically assessing variations in acquisition timelines and the efficacy of instructional interventions.

Bloom filter-based structures, including hash maps and hash tables, are well-established for their space efficiency and speed. However, recent studies indicate that alternative, often underappreciated, filter types can surpass Bloom filters in both velocity and compactness. This paper introduces a detailed analysis of Xor filters, examining their theoretical properties and practical implementations in high-performance quick-access memory systems.
This expository note examines key elements from both convex and complex Hodge theory, highlighting significant parallels and connection points between the two.

This study examines the market directional data generated by the temporal ordering of trading events, where each transaction is defined by its time, execution price, and volume. The research analyzes how this data reacts to the emergence of new information by evaluating the aggregate impact resulting from both individual and collective trades. The analysis focuses on the conditional nature of trading sequences and their impact on subsequent price movements. The methodology involves analyzing the first and second conditional moments of future returns, utilizing the joint distribution of subsequent returns and subsequent trades over various time horizons. The findings indicate that while the market's first moment exhibits a slight negative bias immediately following news events, the second moment experiences significant increases during these periods. These results demonstrate that trading activity is neither random nor impact-free; instead, transactions are order-dependent, meaning their sequence influences future market outcomes.

While federated learning (FL) has emerged as a leading privacy-preserving machine learning framework, FL's standard operation remains vulnerable to specific attacks, such as membership inference and poisoning. Consequently, this paper introduces FLVoogd, a novel framework designed to simultaneously protect privacy and ensure robustness during the federated training process. FLVoogd integrates the Voogd algorithm into the FL workflow to achieve robust model aggregation and employs encryption methods to safeguard data transmission across the network. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications, such as cancer classification, demonstrate that FLVoogd delivers superior robustness and significantly lowers computational overhead compared to current state-of-the-art solutions.

This paper introduces a novel, reinforcement learning-based approach to bridge the Sim2Real gap for autonomous driving, utilizing neural network guidance to adapt robot policies from simulation to reality. By leveraging gradient information within learning algorithms, our method enhances the generalization of policies when deployed in real-world settings. The effectiveness of this technique has been validated through extensive testing on both the nuScenes and Waymo Open datasets.

Deepfake technology, which merges deep learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs), enables the creation of media that is indistinguishable from reality. This capability threatens individual privacy and societal stability, prompting significant interest in understanding the risks across various formats like images, audio, and video. This paper examines the resilience of current detection methods against state-of-the-art deepfake models using unrestricted datasets, specifically 4K and 8K resolution videos. The authors test resilience across multiple codecs and bitrates, revealing a critical weakness: detections based on media-specific artifacts perform poorly on unrecognized content, whereas those relying on algorithmic traces remain more robust. To address this, the study introduces a new, open-source 8K video generation pipeline utilizing a fresh GAN architecture alongside a comprehensive evaluation by leading industry detection algorithms.

Recent studies have revealed that the atmospheres of many exoplanets possess cloudy skies, a finding that has prompted extensive theoretical work on the resulting transit variations. However, this body of literature often overlooks the impact of clouds formed from highly soluble compounds. In this study, we demonstrate that the pre-transit and post-transit environments experience pressure and temperature shifts sufficient to alter the atmospheric chemical equilibrium, specifically triggering the formation of soluble condensates. We illustrate this mechanism by modeling the atmospheres of two temperate sub-Neptune planets, TRAPPIST-1b and K2-18b, focusing on the behavior of water and methane. Our models reveal that the gas-phase abundances of these species undergo significant changes due to the redistribution of heat and the dynamic mixing inherent to the planetary day-night cycles. Consequently, the abundance fluctuations of solutes prior to and following transit differ markedly from the distributions governed solely by thermal equilibrium, a discrepancy that can be detected through transit observations. We argue that future monitoring of exoplanetary transits must incorporate the kinetics of solubility equilibria alongside gas-phase thermochemistry to accurately derive atmospheric compositions.

This research investigates applying efferent (recurrent) spiking neural networks to learn biological sequences, such as food chains and ecological networks, with a specific focus on whether their intrinsic biophysical constraints impede sequence acquisition. The study utilizes an integrated model combining dynamic global connectivity, global neuromodulation, and biologically realistic neuron and synapse characteristics. The work first establishes that these networks can indeed master sequential tasks in an abstract context. The study then demonstrates that the networks can internalize specific traits inherent to real-world food webs, notably efferent connectivity patterns and neuromodulatory mechanisms. The ultimate goal is to construct a computationally efficient, biologically plausible system capable of emulating sequential dynamics found in actual biological environments.

This paper introduces the "Out-of-Category" challenge, a novel framework for assessing semantic segmentation by forcing models to handle scenarios where the target class is absent from their training data. To address the scarcity of real-world examples, the authors developed the In-Category/Out-of-Ca (ICU OC) dataset, which is constructed by randomly masking objects within images from the BDD10K set. They also propose a training methodology that significantly boosts performance on both binary and multi-class segmentation tasks, particularly in detecting occluded regions and classes that were never seen during training.

This study introduces a general framework for the error monitoring of stochastic models utilizing chaos expansions, with a specific focus on the spectral stochastic finite element method (SSFEM). The approach begins by deriving a variational formulation for stochastic models, which positions the random field as random coefficients within the corresponding deterministic counterpart. By separating spatial randomness into deterministic polynomial bases and random coefficients, the methodology transforms the stochastic problem into one. This transformation allows for the application of specific strategies to assess approximation accuracy.

The proposed verification method centers on ensuring that the SSC-resolved deterministic system's solution adheres to the required smoothness dictated by Sobolev imbedding theorems. To support this, the paper presents a comprehensive analysis of random coefficient regularity, deriving new conditions based on the input data's smoothness and the random field's probability measure. Furthermore, the accuracy of the solution is evaluated by comparing it against the exact solution of the deterministic deterministic problem.

Specific techniques for this comparison include an anti-anti-adjoint approach, which generates upper and lower bound estimates, and the adjoint-weighted residual method, which produces single-point error predictions. These verification procedures are demonstrated through various numerical examples.

This study addresses a sequential identification challenge in a partially-observed system where a system's state is only partially accessible, and a change alters the underlying stochastic process. The objective is to detect this shift and, upon confirmation, collect a predefined amount of post-change data before stopping the monitoring procedure. To achieve this, we introduce a new algorithm that leverages control chart techniques for detection and a fixed sample size scheme for verification. We establish the optimality of this proposed method within the framework of average detection delay (ADD) for second-order Markov chains. Additionally, our framework is demonstrated through an application in detecting mean shifts during the monitoring of a specific queueing system.

We investigate the star formation and star metallicity evolution of 12 dwarf galaxies by analyzing their integrated chemical abundance patterns. These dwarfs were selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) to exhibit significant scatter in Mg/Fe ratios, a characteristic often linked to the formation of massive Population III stars. By applying a chemical evolution model, we derive the star formation and initial Population III mass for each galaxy. The results indicate that the majority of these systems began with a very massive Population III component, exceeding 100 solar masses, and experienced a prolonged star formation history, often extending beyond 10 billion years.

Let $G$ be a profinite group; this text introduces $\mathbb{Z}_p[G]$, a homotopy action spectrum for $G$-spaces that functions as a profinite group analogue to the classical complex group ring spectrum.

Extracting structured information from visual documents, such as invoices and receipts, is vital for numerous business applications. While deep learning models have largely replaced traditional methods for this task, they demand large volumes of labeled training data, which is both expensive and labor-intensive to create. This study introduces a zero-shot pre-training strategy that leverages readily available unlabelled archival records to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Consequently, these models require significantly fewer task-specific labeled examples for fine-tuning, thereby enhancing the accessibility and cost-effectiveness of deploying visual document extraction systems.

The europium hexavalent sulfide/indium antimonide (EuS/InAs) interface is a promising candidate for developing magnetic tunnel junctions that support both room-temperature operation and quantum spin Hall effects. Using *ab initio* calculations, this study examines how electronic properties at the interface vary based on specific linking configurations. Results show that interface states within the EuS conduction band gap are primarily formed by Eu-5f and In-4p states, with their positions in the InAs band gap dictated by the structural arrangement. Furthermore, suitable interface states exist within InAs's band gap, indicating potential for induced magnetism in InAs at the interface. These findings suggest that tuning the structural configuration could enable controlled magnetism in the EuS/InAs system.

Although neural network pruning has gained significant attention for accelerating inference, achieving comparable gains in training efficiency and model accuracy remains elusive. We introduce ClickTrain, an end-to-end fine-grained architecture-preserving pruning and training framework designed to accelerate deep learning training while maintaining high model precision. ClickTrain operates by dynamically monitoring the distribution of operations and activations to identify redundant computations, subsequently triggering fine-grained fine-tuned pruning decisions. These decisions result in progressively smaller networks that benefit from trained sparsity, leading to more stable gradient flows and enhanced generalization. Furthermore, the framework employs an efficient fine-grained reparameterization technique to enable the continuous back-propagation of gradients through the progressively pruned network structure. Experiments on various computer vision benchmarks demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves an average speed-up of 3.9× across different models and datasets, with corresponding accuracy improvements of 12.8 MB in average model size.

We examine axioms for modal operators within the complete distributive nonassociative modal logic framework, achieving soundness and completeness over a two-dimensional grid when paired with a spatial modality.

Neutron star-Black hole (NSBH) mergers represent a newly identified class of compact object mergers confirmed by gravitational-wave detectors. These events generate complex waveforms that are difficult to interpret, especially when arising from uncertain physical origins. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify and classify NSBH merger signals. The model successfully achieves high accuracy in identifying signals and determining their properties, including a 99.9% accuracy in classifying spin configurations. Additionally, the framework demonstrates robust performance across diverse signal-to-noise ratios and detector sensitivity levels. Notably, the approach requires minimal computational resources, making it highly suitable for real-time applications.

We report the discovery of an exoplanet, TOI-5542 b, identified via a combination of TESS photometry, high-precision radial velocity (RV) follow-up using HARPS, and astrometric data from Gaia DR3. This system is notable for its host star, a metal-poor G-dwarf with a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.14 ± 0.09 and an age estimated between 8.2 and 13.6 billion years. The planet itself is a gas giant with a minimum mass of 0.51 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ orbiting at 0.061 au with a period of 11.1 days. Its equilibrium temperature stands at 1400 K, and its density is calculated to be 0.69 ± 0.12 g cm$^{-3}$. TOI-5542 b represents the first confirmed exoplanet discovered in a metal-poor system and is comparable in age to the well-known TRAPPIST-1 system. Furthermore, it is one of the oldest known planets orbiting a G-type star. The study concludes that the correlation between planetary mass and stellar metallicity is likely driven by the core accretion mechanism, which requires a substantial dust reservoir to initiate core formation, whereas the subsequent gas accretion phase is not strictly dependent on metallicity.

We introduce a primal–dual algorithm designed to solve the dynamic programming equations associated with constrained Markov decision processes (MDPs), which can be viewed as extending the Lagrange multiplier method for reward-maximization problems to cases involving multiple constraints. Although constraints in standard MDPs are typically limited to a finite set of conditions regarding stationary distributions, this work generalizes the problem to scenarios involving continuous-time transitions with potentially uncountable constraints. We establish the convergence of proposed iterations toward the primal–dual optimal solution under mild assumptions, with convergence rates of $1/T$ for both sampled trajectories and full expectation scenarios. Furthermore, we present a sampled version utilizing importance sampling that achieves $1/T$ convergence, supported by theoretical upper bounds on both sample-dependent and sample-averaged excess costs.

This paper outlines a methodology for offline recognition of handwritten mathematical notation through deep learning, aiming to bridge a critical gap since current software like Microsoft Math Solver and Google's Math Assistant focus primarily on optical recognition and numerical computation of known equations. We introduce a solution capable of identifying notation across the full spectrum from small components, such as operators and variables, to complex structures like integrals and summations, by training on extensive datasets of notation images.

We introduce a novel application of the Witten complex to a general quantum mechanical model where a superpotential is an arbitrary polynomial. In this framework, non-trapped run-away dynamics drives the sheaf cohomology of an associated differential geometric space, leading to a step-by-step calculation of sheaf cohomology groups. This process is governed by the progressive degeneration of the supersymmetric charge algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sheaf cohomology groups—representing the zero-eigenvalue subspace of quantum mechanics—are equivalently determined by the non-negative-eigenvalue subspace through the action of the superpotential.

Networks serve as a foundational framework for modeling inter-entity interactions in complex systems, ranging from global trade and financial markets to social structures and biological models. While existing research has extensively covered the statistical traits of these networks, they frequently overlook the variability inherent in the specific entities and temporal sequences involved in interactions. This study investigates the fluctuation of energy exchange between interconnected nodes in a complex network, applying a method analogous to analyzing fluctuations in heat produced by fluctuating currents. Our results demonstrate that interaction variability adheres to universal scaling laws, with interaction variability itself following a $\ln(\tau)$ distribution. Additionally, we examine how the mean and fluctuating components of energy exchange relate to one another, observing that their correlation is significantly influenced by network topology. Notably, in both Erdős–Rény (ER) models and scale-free structures, the relationship between energy exchange's mean and variance remains consistent across different parameters, leading us to propose that this energy exchange variability exhibits universal characteristics.

Actor-critical Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a prominent framework for addressing sequential decision-making challenges. However, its efficacy is often hindered by sample inefficiency and policy collapse. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a novel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)-based approach designed to enhance sample utilization through more efficient parameter sampling. Our method implements Hamiltonian dynamics within the actor's neural network to execute Hamiltonian Monte Carlo updates directly within RL, thereby boosting the algorithm's sample efficiency. Furthermore, we establish theoretical proof that this HMC-integrated hybrid RL model successfully narrows the policy gap, effectively preventing policy degradation. Empirical evaluations across various environments demonstrate that our method not only enhances performance but also establishes new state-of-the-art benchmarks.

Dynamic treatment regimes are time-versional decision-making frameworks where choices at each step depend on the current state and prior actions. While previous research has addressed learning these regimes using historical data in both Markov and non-Markov settings, the uncertainty inherent in this process often results in suboptimal performance during the data collection phase. This study introduces a Bayesian learning method specifically for continuous-time Markov decision problems, aiming to maximize the cumulative negatity—a comprehensive utility metric that accounts for the entire treatment trajectory. By employing a Bayesian framework, the regime's parameters are modeled as random variables with an assigned prior distribution; this prior is subsequently updated via posterior inference as new data becomes available. The resulting regime is optimized by maximizing the posterior expected negativity. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a Bayesian analysis of real-world historical data concerning hormone replacement therapy for post-menopausal women.

We introduce a novel form of duality applicable to any pair of dual vector spaces, manifesting as a correspondence between certain (bi-)graded modules arising from the tensor algebra of one space and specific graded modules derived from the commutator algebra of the other. This framework generalizes known homological dualities that apply when spaces are in "partial resolution" of each other, such as being free or having a cellular basis, and it encompasses both Borel-Moede cellular homology and Calkin-Weil stratification cell homology within its scope.

We introduce a new method for generating finite sets of quantum measurement configurations, utilizing complex $E_8$ as the underlying system. The real vector space $V$ associated with the $E_8$ root system has the dimension 240, and its root set $\Phi$ is defined as the collection of all vectors with length squared equal to 2.
